title: Court Ruling A Roadblock To West Virginia Charter Schools
author: Peter Greene
summary: A West Virginia court ruled that charter school authorizations must require voter approval in counties where they would operate, restoring local democratic control. The case challenged whether the state's Professional Charter School Board (appointed by the governor) could bypass local school boards and voters, arguing that the state constitution requires electoral consent for new school districts. The ruling reasserts that foundational governance structures are enforceable limits on executive authority, not ceremonial provisions, and reflects an enduring tension between state-level policy and local democratic accountability.
points: Democracy in school design: Charter expansion is legitimate but must respect voters' right to consent when new schools are created.
Constitutional limits bind power: Appointed state bodies cannot override electoral requirements, even with good-faith policy arguments.
Local voice reasserts itself: The ruling transfers authority back to communities and their elected boards.
quotes: On December 3, Kanawha Circuit Judge Jennifer Bailey issued a permanent injunction that prevents the West Virginia Professional Charter School Board from authorizing any new charter schools without the approval of the voters in the county where the charter wants to do business.

West Virginia's constitution offers a clear statement about establishing new schools: No independent free school district, or organization shall hereafter be created, except with the consent of the school district or districts out of which the same is to be created, expressed by a majority of the voters voting on the question.

In 2021, the state modified the charter law. The bill turned every mention of 'charter school' into 'public charter school,' and it created the West Virginia Professional Charter School Board, a new path for charter authorization. The board members are appointed by the governor, and they had the power to authorize a charter school anywhere in the state, even if that charter had been previously rejected by the local elected school board.

The law was challenged in court in 2021 by Sam Brunett and Robert McCloud. Their lawsuit did not challenge the effectiveness of charter schools, but argued that the new approval process violated the state constitution.
Local elected school boards can be reluctant to open up competing schools funded with local taxpayer dollars.” Archived from Curmudgucation on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
